entries.name: Brook trout
entries.migrates: some populations move between stream and lake
behaviour: char of cold clear headwater streams and spring brooks
bite readily on small dry flies and nymphs
hybridizes with introduced rainbow trout

voxel_model.pattern: vermiculation on back; white-edged pectoral fins; red spots with blue halos

entries.notes: The default fish of the small shaded stream; eastern North America's native char, widely stocked. Its presence marks cold, clean, unsilted water.

entries.name: Brown trout
entries.migrates: some sea-run ('sea trout') and lake-run ('ferox') forms
behaviour: wary and nocturnal in pressured waters
eats small mammals off the surface at night
native to the Atlantic basin, introduced nearly everywhere trout fishing exists

voxel_model.pattern: golden-brown flanks with black and red spots

entries.notes: The classic wary stream trout of Europe; catching a big one demands stealth. Native across Atlantic Europe and North Africa, now global.

entries.name: Rainbow trout
behaviour: leaps spectacularly when hooked
native to the Pacific coast of North America and Asia
farmed and stocked worldwide, often dominant over native trout

voxel_model.pattern: pink flank band, dense black spotting on body and tail

entries.notes: Steelhead, when anadromous, is the ocean-going trophy form of the same species. Leaping rainbows are the postcard of trout streams.

entries.name: Cutthroat trout
entries.migrates: some populations migratory between stream and lake
behaviour: takes dry flies enthusiastically, even in bright light
the only trout with a red slash beneath the jaw
many subspecies are genetically distinct and range-limited

voxel_model.pattern: orange-red slash on lower jaw; heavy tail spotting

entries.notes: The native trout of the American West's small streams; conservation of its many subspecies is a running battle with introduced rainbows.

entries.name: European grayling
behaviour: males raise a huge sail-like dorsal fin during courtship
rises to dry flies like a trout, but on clear chalk-stream glides
classic chalk-stream and limestone-river fish

voxel_model.pattern: oversized spotted dorsal fin; violet flank flush

entries.notes: The 'lady of the stream', with the biggest dorsal fin relative to body of any European fish. Wild grayling are a sign of clean limestone water.

entries.name: Common minnow
behaviour: forms shoals that flash in shallow riffles
males turn bright red and blue-black in breeding dress
classic bait and biological indicator of good water

voxel_model.pattern: dark lateral band; breeding males flush scarlet

entries.notes: Europe's pocket-sized stream fish, the first thing a child catches. Shoals turn any clear brook into a moving disco in May.

entries.name: Blacknose dace
behaviour: thrives in the tiniest headwater trickles where little else survives
tolerates silt and pollution better than most natives
mottled camouflage blends into stony riffles

voxel_model.pattern: dark mottling; dusky lateral stripe through the eye

entries.notes: The fish of the smallest creeks, persisting where the water barely covers its back. A workhorse species for colonizing headwaters.

entries.name: Three-spined stickleback
behaviour: males build a glue-bound nest of plant matter and guard eggs and fry
three stout dorsal spines lock erect against predators
textbook case of rapid evolution; benthic and limnetic pairs speciated in isolated lakes

voxel_model.pattern: breeding males: red throat and belly, blue eyes

entries.notes: The darling of evolutionary biology: populations repeatedly evolved distinct benthic and limnetic forms within isolated lakes in centuries.

entries.name: European bullhead
behaviour: broad flat head hides between stones by day
no swim bladder; scuttles along the bed rather than swimming
indicator of very clean, well-oxygenated stony streams

voxel_model.pattern: mottled brown; oversized head with wide mouth

entries.notes: The miller's thumb of English rhyme: a pebble-mimicking bottom fish you only notice when you turn over a stone.

entries.name: Brook lamprey
behaviour: leaf-eating larva (ammocoete) filter-feeds for years in silt before metamorphosis
adults never eat; they spawn in gravel riffles and die
jawless, with a sucker-like round mouth of horny teeth

voxel_model.pattern: eel-like body; circular sucking mouth

entries.notes: A jawless fish from before the age of jaws. Unlike its parasitic sea cousin, it feeds only as a larva and serves as a trout staple.

entries.name: Guppy
behaviour: livebearer; females brood young internally every few weeks
males are living jewelry, and females remember which ones harass them
Trinidad's streams are the world's natural laboratory for predator-driven evolution

voxel_model.pattern: males: rainbow-mosaic tail and body; females drab

entries.notes: The million-fish of the aquarium trade; in the wild, Caroni drainage guppies change colour in response to pike-cichlid predation within generations.

entries.name: Common frog
entries.migrates: short hops to ancestral spawning ponds in spring
behaviour: explosive mass spawnings: clumps of thousands of eggs appear overnight
terrestrial most of the year, returning to water only to breed
survives near-freezing by flooding its tissues with glucose antifreeze

voxel_model.pattern: variable brown/olive; dark mask behind eye; temporal patch

entries.notes: The archetypal garden frog of European streams and ditches; its spawn clumps are the first sure sign of spring.

entries.name: Common toad
entries.migrates: mass processions to breeding ponds on the first warm wet nights of spring
behaviour: walks rather than hops, strings of eggs wrapped around submerged stems
warty parotoid glands ooze bufotoxin that makes it taste foul
can live decades, digging itself into soft earth for winter
sounds: high-pitched trill from males courting underwater

voxel_model.pattern: warty brown back; golden iris with horizontal pupil

entries.notes: Road-crossing masses each spring are a folk ritual; many local groups organize toad patrols to carry them across.

entries.name: Smooth newt
entries.migrates: short seasonal move from land to water in spring
behaviour: males grow a wavy crest in breeding season and wiggle to flash it at females
terrestrial under logs and leaf litter most of the year
limbs and tail regenerate after loss

voxel_model.pattern: belly mottled orange; male's crest has dark spots

entries.notes: Britain's most familiar newt; egg sacs folded one by one into pondweed leaves are a neat field sign.

entries.name: Fire salamander
behaviour: lives near cold shaded woodland brooks; females release larvae directly into the stream
the yellow-and-black warning pattern advertises samandarin toxins
associated with myth: believed to walk through fire unharmed

voxel_model.pattern: glossy black with bright yellow blotches or stripes

entries.notes: Europe's most vivid amphibian; check mossy stones beside mountain brooks on damp nights. Toxins can sting eyes and mouth.

entries.name: Anson's torrent frog
behaviour: lives on rocks in noisy white water where almost nothing else calls
concave eardrums matched to the pitch of rushing water
call is whisper-quiet, among the faintest frog calls known
sounds: barely audible chirp, tuned to the roar of torrents

voxel_model.pattern: mottled brown, flattened for rock-clinging

entries.notes: Borneo's murmurer: evolved its hearing down to near-silence because its torrent habitat is deafening. Bring a stethoscope, not a headlamp.

entries.name: Mudpuppy
behaviour: keeps its feathery external gills its whole life; never moves ashore
barks when harassed
lingers under flat stones in cool riffles by day

voxel_model.pattern: rusty mottling; bushy red external gills

entries.notes: A permanent larva: adult mudpuppies never metamorphose. Anglers snag them while crayfishing and mistake them for hellish little dogs.

entries.name: Grass snake
behaviour: hisses loudly, flattens its head and gapes when threatened
squirts foul-smelling musk from anal glands
famously 'plays dead' with mouth agape and tongue out

voxel_model.pattern: yellow collar behind the head; round pupils

entries.notes: Completely harmless; the most common snake actually seen near water in Europe. Toads are its staple diet, often caught mid-hop.

entries.name: Northern water snake
behaviour: basks on overhanging branches and drops into the water when disturbed
bites readily and musks; not venomous but mistaken for cottonmouths
gives birth to live young, often in communal basking groups

voxel_model.pattern: dark blotches and bands on brown-grey; keeled scales

entries.notes: The snake Americans most often misidentify as a cottonmouth. A belligerent but venom-free fish-grabber of cattail edges.

entries.name: Belted kingfisher
entries.migrates: northern populations migrate south of freezing waters
behaviour: perches on wires and snags, then drops headfirst to stab fish
excavates a tunnel nest in steep sandy banks, often over water
rattles loudly when flushed; the rattling carries a long way

voxel_model.pattern: slate-blue back; females have a rusty double breast band

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. Its rattle is the punctuation mark of every North American creek; burrow nests crumble from undercut banks.

entries.name: Grey wagtail
behaviour: bobs its long tail while walking the water's edge hunting insect larvae
nests in mossy crevices behind waterfalls and under bridges
both sexes flash a brilliant lemon-yellow rump in flight
sounds: thin 'tsip' calls; a silvery tinkling song

voxel_model.pattern: grey back, yellow belly, very long tail

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The sign that the stream is alive: it works the current all day, utterly unafraid of people.

entries.name: American dipper
behaviour: wades, swims and walks underwater against white-water torrents
bobs emphatically on a rock before each dive
builds a domed moss nest behind waterfalls

voxel_model.pattern: sooty brown body, flashing white eyelid

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The western cousin of the Eurasian dipper; the only songbird in the Americas that feeds underwater.

entries.name: White wagtail
behaviour: wags its long black-and-white tail non-stop while striding along gravel bars
nests in crevices of bridges, walls and rock piles
Britain's pied form is the national 'wagtail of the towpath'

voxel_model.pattern: bold black bib, cap and back; white face and belly

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The most familiar walking bird along every stream path and bridge in the Old World.

entries.name: Eurasian water shrew
behaviour: dives like a furred torpedo, rows with fringed hind-feet
saliva carries a mild venom that subdues prey larger than itself
roosts in bank holes; its rapid high-pitched squeaking is a quiet-stream signature

voxel_model.pattern: dark above, silvery below; white-fringed hind feet

entries.notes: A venomous, swimming shrew two body-lengths from your ankle. Look for its tiny four-toed tracks and dive-holes on muddy banks.

entries.name: Water vole
behaviour: perfectly round blunt nose, small round ears, blunt furry tail
feeds at the bank edge and 'plops' into the water when startled
the real-life Ratty of The Wind in the Willows; crashes followed mink's arrival

voxel_model.pattern: chestnut-brown fur, blunt face, furry ears barely visible

entries.notes: Bright-eyed, fat-cheeked and splashy; a keystone prey for mink. Its absence from a stretch of bank is an ecological alarm bell.

entries.name: American mink
behaviour: sleek semiaquatic hunter, den in bank burrows and rock cavities
delayed implantation; mating in late winter, kits in late spring
escaped fur-farm animals have naturalized across Europe, hammering water voles

voxel_model.pattern: dark chocolate fur, white chin and chest patch

entries.notes: gestation_days is delayed-implantation; true gestation ~40-75 days. In Europe an invasive nuisance; in America, simply the mink.

entries.name: Star-nosed mole
behaviour: nose ringed by 22 fleshy tentacles, the fastest touch organ known
may 'eat' 10-12 times per second; can smell underwater by blowing bubbles
tunnels into marshy banks and paddles on the surface of small streams

voxel_model.pattern: pink star of 22 tentacles on snout tip

entries.notes: The fastest-eating mammal ever measured, and one of only two mammal species known to smell underwater. Pure wet-meadow strangeness.

entries.name: Pyrenean desman
behaviour: half aquatic mole with a trunk-like sensitive snout
broad webbed hind feet and a flattened rudder tail for swimming
declining fast; threatened by river engineering and introduced American mink

voxel_model.pattern: velvety dark fur; long laterally-flattened tail

entries.notes: A relict survivor of the Pyrenees' cold rocky streams, found nowhere else on Earth. Every engineered or mink-infested stretch loses them.

entries.name: Banded demoiselle
behaviour: males are brilliant metallic blue-green with a dark wing band, helicoptering over the water
females are translucent green and flick their wings in response
larvae live a year in the silt before emerging; needs rich riverside vegetation

voxel_model.pattern: males: iridescent turquoise body, dark wing bands

entries.notes: The closest thing a slow warm stream has to a jewel; density of males along a weedy margin is a quick habitat quality check.

entries.name: Dobsonfly
behaviour: larvae ('hellgrammites') live 2-3 years in streams and are unbeatable bait
males carry tusk-like mandibles longer than their head; they cannot bite, only pinch
adults shelter under bridges and bark near the water by day

voxel_model.pattern: smoky wings with dark veins; male tusks

entries.notes: The Hellgrammite Fishery: turn a rock in a clean stream and you'll find the larva; hang it on a hook and trout go mad.

entries.name: Green drake mayfly
behaviour: larvae burrow for years in stream silt, pumping water through their gills
mass emergences ('hatches') bring trout rising madly
adults live a day or two, flying upstream to mate in dancing swarms

voxel_model.pattern: yellow-olive body, dusky wings, three tails

entries.notes: The fly-fisher's grail: the green drake hatch turns sedate chalk streams into feeding frenzies for a few days in June.

entries.name: Golden stonefly
behaviour: nymphs hunt other nymphs under stones, needing very clean fast water
adults crawl out of the water to molt; bad flyers, easy prey
salmonids key on the golden hatch; 'golden stones' are western fly-fishing staples

voxel_model.pattern: golden-brown wings folded flat over the back

entries.notes: A stonefly-sized dinner bell for trout: if the golden stoneflies hatch, the river is healthy and the fishing is on.

entries.name: Freshwater shrimp (scud)
behaviour: sideways-swimming amphipod swarming under stones and leaf packs
shreds fallen leaves into the food web
its presence and sensitivity make it a standard water-quality indicator

voxel_model.pattern: translucent beige, shrimp-arched

entries.notes: The crumbs of the stream: without Gammarus shredding leaf litter, the whole trout food chain stalls.

entries.name: Signal crayfish
behaviour: white blaze at the claw joint 'signals' at rivals; native to the Pacific Northwest
formidable claws, outcompetes Europe's noble crayfish and carries crayfish plague
burrows into banks and eats everything, alive or dead

voxel_model.pattern: smooth chestnut shell; white signal patch at claw joint

entries.notes: Introduced for farming and escaped everywhere; in Europe a walking plague battery. A single berried female colonizes a new reach.

entries.name: Freshwater pearl mussel
behaviour: students have aged specimens over 250 years; growth ring counting is a dark art
larvae (glochidia) clamp onto trout and salmon gills to disperse
needs the cleanest, coolest, most stable streams; vanished from most of its old range

voxel_model.pattern: dark loaf-shaped river shells half-buried in clean gravel

entries.player: protected in most of its range; tamable: no
entries.notes: A living time capsule, a century per mussel; a stream with pearl mussels is a stream in near-pristine health. Historical 'pearl rushes' stripped many beds.

entries.name: Ramshorn snail
behaviour: flat spiral shell like a tiny coiled ram's horn, laid in jelly masses on stems
hermaphrodite; breathes air at the surface through an open mantle cavity
scrapes algae off stones and plants with a ribbon-like radula

voxel_model.pattern: reddish-brown flat-coiled shell

entries.notes: The commonest pond-snail-on-a-string at the slow edges; harmless, decorative, and excellent at keeping glass clean.
